etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English webbe, from Old English webb, from Proto-Germanic *wabją, from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ- (“weave”).

definitions.definition: The silken structure which a spider builds using silk secreted from the spinnerets at the caudal tip of its abdomen; a spiderweb.
(by extension) Any interconnected set of persons, places, or things, which, when diagrammed, resembles a spider's web.

quote.citation: 1828, Washington Irving, “Birth, Parentage, and Education of Columbus”, in A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus. […], volume I, New York, N.Y.: G. & C. Carvill, […], →OCLC, book I, page 3:
quote.text: The time of his birth, his birth-place, his parentage, are all involved in obscurity; and such has been the perplexing ingenuity of commentators, that it is difficult to extricate the truth from the web of conjectures with which it is interwoven.

quote.citation: 1851 (indicated as 1852), Nathaniel Hawthorne, “Main-Street”, in The Snow-Image, and Other Twice-Told Tales, Boston, Mass.: Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, →OCLC, page 96:
quote.text: [T]he blame must rest on the sombre spirit of our forefathers, who wove their web of life with hardly a single thread of rose-color or gold, and not on me, who have a tropic-love of sunshine, and would gladly gild all the world with it, if I knew where to find so much.

quote.citation: 2018 February 14, Dan Shive, El Goonish Shive (webcomic), Comic for Wednesday, Feb 14, 2018:
quote.text: "But THAT!  Was the OLDEN TIMES!  A massive, worldwide web of global information has ENTANGLED THE WORLD!  People in Beijing can read about a magical incident in Moperville in seconds, and have video of it in minutes!"

definitions.definition: (baseball) The part of a baseball mitt between the forefinger and thumb, the webbing.
A latticed or woven structure.

quote.citation: 1866, George Bancroft, “New Netherland”, in History of the United States of America, from the Discovery of the American Continent, 21st edition, volume II, Boston: Little, Brown, and Company, page 281:
quote.text: The colonists were forbidden to manufacture any woollen, or linen, or cotton fabrics ; not a web might be woven, not a shuttle thrown, on penalty of exile.

definitions.definition: (usually with "spin", "weave", or similar verbs) A tall tale with more complexity than a myth or legend.
A plot or scheme.
The interconnection between flanges in structural members, increasing the effective lever arm and so the load capacity of the member.
(rail transport) The thinner vertical section of a railway rail between the top (head) and bottom (foot) of the rail.
A fold of tissue connecting the toes of certain birds, or of other animals.
The series of barbs implanted on each side of the shaft of a feather, whether stiff and united together by barbules, as in ordinary feathers, or soft and separate, as in downy feathers.
(manufacturing) A continuous strip of material carried by rollers during processing.
(lithography) A long sheet of paper which is fed from a roll into a printing press, as opposed to individual sheets of paper.
(glassblowing, obsolete) A seventeenth-century unit of Rhenish glass containing 60 bunches.
(dated) A band of webbing used to regulate the extension of the hood of a carriage.
The blade of a sword.

quote.citation: 1600, [Torquato Tasso], “The Second Booke of Godfrey of Bulloigne”, in Edward Fairefax [i.e., Edward Fairfax], transl., Godfrey of Bulloigne, or The Recouerie of Ierusalem. […], London:  […]  Ar[nold] Hatfield, for I[saac] Iaggard and M[atthew] Lownes, →OCLC, stanza 93, page 38:
quote.text: Argant a ſword, whereof the web was ſteele, / Pommell, rich ſtone ; hilts, gold, approu’d by tuch, / With rareſt workmanſhip all forged weele, / The curious art exceld the ſubſtance much.

definitions.definition: The blade of a saw.
The thin, sharp part of a colter.
The bit of a key.
A thin metal sheet, plate, or strip, as of lead.

quote.citation: 1600, [Torquato Tasso], “The Tenth Booke of Godfrey of Bulloigne”, in Edward Fairefax [i.e., Edward Fairfax], transl., Godfrey of Bulloigne, or The Recouerie of Ierusalem. […], London:  […]  Ar[nold] Hatfield, for I[saac] Iaggard and M[atthew] Lownes, →OCLC, stanza 26, page 184:
quote.text: […]  And there with ſtately pompe by heapes they wend, / And Chriſtians ſlaine rolle vp in webs of lead  […]

definitions.definition: (dated, US, radio, television) A major broadcasting network.

quote.text: […]  the first big move toward a contract for television performers was made Friday (20) when the webs agreed to pay them according to the length of the show.  […]  Altho the major TV webs — NBC and CBS — may fall in line soon, an agreement may possibly be held up by the opposition of DuMont  […]

definitions.definition: (architecture) A section of a groin vault, separated by ribs. (Can we clean up(+) this sense?)
(medicine, archaic) A cataract of the eye.
(intransitive) To construct or form a web.
(transitive) To cover with a web or network.

quote.citation: 1853 June 21, R. C. Stone, “A New Insect”, in Simon Brown, editor, The New England Farmer, volume V, Boston: Raynolds & Nourse, page 362:
quote.text: The canker worm has no shelter upon the tree, but lies out upon the leaf or branch ; this forms itself a house by webbing the corner of a leaf, into which it retreats on the first appearance of danger […]

quote.citation: 1895, “Has Gold Risen?”, in The Forum, volume XVIII, New York: The Forum Publishing Co., page 577:
quote.text: In the meantime continents were being ribbed with railways, the atmosphere was being webbed with telegraph wires connecting every important commercial centre […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To ensnare or entangle.
(transitive) To provide with a web.
(transitive, obsolete) To weave.

quote.citation: 1511–12, “An Act agaynst deceyptfull making of Wollen Cloth”, in The Statures of the Realm, volume III, London: Dawsons of Pall Mall, published 1963, page 28:
quote.text: Item that the Wever whiche shall have the wevyng of eny wollen yerne to be webbed into cloth shall weve werk […][paraphrase] Likewise, that the weaver who is to weave any woollen yarn to be woven into cloth shall weave it well.
